subject: Business Models
title: McDonald's: The Real Estate Play
description: A micro-lesson that makes McDonald's: The Real Estate Play usable.

hook.text: McDonald's makes more money from rent than from burgers. It's a real estate company in disguise.

buildup.text: Ray Kroc's advisor told him: 'You're not in the burger business. You're in the real estate business.'

discovery.text: McDonald's buys or leases land, then subleases to franchisees at a markup. Rent is 8-15% of sales.

twist.text: McDonald's owns $40 billion in real estate. Even if every restaurant closed, the land is worth a fortune.

climax.text: Controlling the real estate gives McDonald's leverage. Underperforming franchisees can be replaced easily.

punchline.text: $40 billion in property. The burgers are just the tenants' problem.

quiz.question: How much real estate does McDonald's own?

details.summary: McDonald's real business model is real estate, not hamburgers. The company owns or leases the land and buildings where franchisees operate, collecting rent that often exceeds franchise royalties. This real estate strategy makes McDonald's one of the world's largest property companies.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding McDonald's reveals that the most successful franchise in history generates most of its profit from property ownership, not food sales. The hamburgers are the mechanism that makes the real estate valuable.
takeaways: McDonald's owns the land and buildings where most franchisees operate
Rent from franchisees generates more revenue than food franchise royalties
The real estate portfolio makes McDonald's one of the world's largest property owners

faq.question: How does McDonald's real estate model work?
faq.answer: McDonald's acquires or leases prime locations, then subleases to franchisees at a significant markup. Franchisees pay rent based on a percentage of sales with a minimum floor. This gives McDonald's stable rental income that increases as store revenues grow.

faq.question: Why is McDonald's real estate strategy so profitable?
faq.answer: McDonald's negotiates bulk real estate deals at favorable rates and subleases at higher rates. The rental income is more predictable than food sales. Property values appreciate over time. The company controls locations so franchisees cannot take them to a competitor brand.
